entities.summary:
Zeami Motokiyo , also called Kanze Motokiyo , was a Japanese aesthetician, actor, and playwright who played a pivotal role in the development of Noh theatre during the Muromachi period (1336-1573). Born into a family of actors, he was trained in the art of Noh from a young age and became a renowned performer and playwright. His works, including the Noh play 'Shinju Yori Monogatari', are still performed today and provide valuable insights into the aesthetics and philosophy of the time.

Zeami's contributions to the world of Noh theatre had a lasting impact on the development of Japanese drama and theatre. His emphasis on the importance of emotion, movement, and the human condition helped shape the aesthetic of Noh and influenced generations of performers and playwrights. As a result, his legacy continues to be celebrated and studied by scholars and theatre enthusiasts around the world.

One of the most significant aspects of Zeami's work is his concept of 'honne' and 'tatemae', which refers to the distinction between a person's true feelings and the social norms they are expected to follow. This concept is still widely studied and debated today, and its relevance extends beyond the realm of theatre to the broader human experience.

Zeami's life and work also provide valuable insights into the cultural and historical context of the Muromachi period, a time of great social, economic, and political change in Japan. His writings and performances offer a unique window into the values, beliefs, and practices of the time, and have helped shape our understanding of this fascinating period in Japanese history.

In conclusion, Zeami Motokiyo's contributions to Noh theatre and Japanese drama are undeniable, and his legacy continues to inspire and influence artists, scholars, and enthusiasts to this day.
